<comment datatype="string"><a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=2-O-ALPHA-MANNOSYL-D-GLYCERATE">Mannosylglycerate</a> (MG) is an osmolyte utilized by hyperthermophilic archaea and bacteria (see MetaCyc pathway <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-5656">mannosylglycerate biosynthesis I</a>). 
<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a> is able to utilize MG as a carbon source but not as protection against osmotic stress.
<p>
MG utilization is controlled by the divergently transcribed <I>mngR</I> gene and <I>mngAB</I> operon. 
MngR acts as a repressor of the expression both <I>mngR</I> and <I>mngAB</I>. 
MngA is the EII component of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-2.7.1.195">EC 2.7.1.195, protein-<em>N</em><small><sup>&pi;</sup></small>-phosphohistidine&mdash;2-<em>O</em>-&alpha;-mannosyl-<small>D</small>-glycerate phosphotransferase</a>, a PEP-dependent sugar phosphotransferase system responsible for the uptake and phosphorylation of MG to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-1063">2-<I>O</I>-(6-phospho-&alpha;-D-mannosyl)-D-glycerate</a>, which is subsequently hydrolyzed to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=MANNOSE-6P">&alpha;-D-mannopyranose 6-phosphate</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=GLYCERATE">D-glycerate</a> by the <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=EG13236-MONOMER">&alpha;-mannosidase</a> MngB.  <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=GLYCERATE">D-glycerate</a> can be converted to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=2-PG">2-phospho-D-glycerate</a> by <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=GKI-MONOMER">glycerate 2-kinase 1</a> encoded by the <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=EG11175">garK</a> gene, which is also induced when cells are grown in MG [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14645248">Sampaio04</a>].</comment>

<comment datatype="string">2-O-&alpha;-Mannosyl-D-glycerate (MG) is an osmolyte utilized by hyperthermophilic archaea and
bacteria (see MetaCyc pathway <a href="http://biocyc.org/META/new-image?object=PWY-5656">mannosylglycerate biosynthesis I</a>). 
<I>E. coli</I> is able to utilize MG as a carbon source but not as protection against osmotic stress. 
MG utilization is controlled by the divergently transcribed <I>mngR</I> gene and <I>mngAB</I> operon. 
MngR acts as a repressor of the expression both <I>mngR</I> and <I>mngAB</I>. 
MngA is the EII of a PEP-dependent sugar phosphotransferase system responsible for the
uptake and phosphorylation of MG to 2-O-(6-phospho-&alpha;-mannosyl)-D-glycerate,
which is subsequently converted to mannose-6-phosphate and glycerate by the
&alpha;-mannosidase MngB.  Glycerate can be converted to 2-phosphoglycerate by
glycerate kinase I encoded by the <I>garK</I> gene which is also induced when cells
are grown in MG. [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14645248">Sampaio04</a>]</comment>

<comment datatype="string">PtsI (Enzyme I) is a cytoplasmic protein that serves as the gateway for the phosphoenolpyruvate:sugar phosphotransferase system (PTS<sup>sugar</sup>). PtsI is one of two (PtsI and PtsH) sugar non-specific protein constituents of the PTS<sup>sugar</sup> which along with a sugar-specific inner membrane permease effect a phosphotransfer cascade that results in the coupled phosphorylation and transport of a variety of carbohydrate substrates.
<p>
PtsI purifies as a monomer and a homodimer; PtsI accepts a phosphoryl group from phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP) - on histidine residue 189 - and transfers it to the low molecular weight phosphocarrier protein HPr (also known as PtsH); activity requires the homodimeric form of PtsI and the presence of a divalent metal ion (Mg2+) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14224387">Kundig64</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6992959">Waygood80</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6986909">Misset80</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7049236">Hoving82</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3316210">Neyroz87</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33277485">Hu20</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35636362">Hu22</a>]. The monomer/dimer transition may play a role in regulating PtsI activity [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8051118">Chauvin94</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8051119">Chauvin94a</a>]. The PtsI dimer accepts one phosphoryl group per subunit; the rate of dimerization is slow compared to the rate of phosphorylation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16171394">Meadow05a</a>]
<p>
The PtsI monomer consists of a protease resistant N-terminal domain (E1N) which contains the active histidine residue and the HPr binding domain, and a C-terminal domain (E1C) which binds PEP and is required for dimerization [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8031118">Lee94f</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8692938">Chauvin96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8805571">Liao96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8552636">Seok96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9109646">Garrett97a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9671705">Fomenkov98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10048929">Garrett99</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17053069">Teplyakov06</a>]. Purified, crystallized E1N consists of a helical HPr binding subdomain and an &alpha;&beta; subdomain that contains the active histidine [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8805571">Liao96</a>]. Purified E1N does not dimerize; purified E1N is phosphorylated by phospho-HPr but not by PEP [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8692938">Chauvin96</a>]. Purified E1C is dimeric and hydrolyses PEP into pyruvate and P<sub><i>i</i></sub>; purified E1C exists in a dynamic equilibrium between open and closed conformation (later referred to as expanded and compact forms); PEP binding stabilizes the compact conformation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22722931">Venditti12</a>]. 
<p>
The catalytic cycle of PtsI is accompanied by large scale interdomain movement [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20731394">Schwieters10</a>]. The interdomain rearrangement associated with the open to closed transition of PtsI is triggered by PEP binding to the C-terminal domain; PEP binding stabilises a rigid (compact) conformation of the C-terminal domain which triggers the open to closed transition of PtsI; the closed conformation of PtsI is consistent with phosphoryl transfer from PEP to His189; phosphorylation of His189 results in interdomain rearrangement which exposes the phosphoryl group and makes it available for transfer to HPr [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25581904">Venditti15</a>].
<p>
PtsI activity is inhibited by <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=2-KETOGLUTARATE">2-oxoglutarate</a> (&alpha;-ketoglutarate); this mechanism provides a regulatory link between central carbon and nitrogen metabolism ensuring that glucose consumption is matched to nitrogen-controlled growth rate; a strain in which the PTS is absent (<i>&Delta;ptsHI &Delta;crr</i>) does not increase glucose uptake following nitrogen upshift indicating that it uncouples glucose consumption from nitrogen status [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22002719">Doucette11</a>]. 2-oxoglutarate inhibits PtsI <i>in vitro</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22002719">Doucette11</a>]; 2-oxoglutarate binds to the active site of PtsI acting as a comptetitive inhibitor of PtsI activity; 2-oxoglutarate interacts with the C-terminal domain of PtsI at the binding site for PEP [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23506042">Venditti13</a>]. Phosphoryl flux through PTS systems (via Enzyme I and HPr) plays a regulatory role in coordinating carbon utilization strategy and more specifically in switching between the two alterative metabolic strategies of hierarchical sugar utilization versus co-utilization [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26784570">Westermayer16</a>].
<p>
PtsI supports pyruvate to phosphoenolpyruvate flux during both gluconeogenic and glycolytic growth; direct phosphorylation of pyruvate by PtsI has not been shown and the identity of the phosphoryl donor is not known [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28128209">Long17</a>].   
<p>
PtsI localizes to the inner surface of the cytoplasmic membrane [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2644649">Ghosh89</a>]. The subcellular distribution of fluorescently labeled PtsI varies from diffuse to punctate to polar depending on growth conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15557553">Patel04c</a>]. Both of the general PTS proteins - PtsI and PtsH - localize mainly near the cell poles, regardless of growth conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20924357">Lopian10</a>] (and further [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24129255">Govindarajan13</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29387047">Govindarajan17</a>]). Localization of PtsI is controlled by <a href="http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/new-image?object=G7087-MONOMER">PTS system regulator TmaR</a>; TmaR-mediated control of PtsI localization impacts PtsI activity and regulates sugar metabolism [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33376208">Szoke21</a>]. PtsI can be phosphorylated at Tyr-122; PtsI lacking Tyr-122 (PtsI Y122F) is not detected in polar clusters [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33376208">Szoke21</a>].
<p>
An <i>E. coli</i> <i>ptsI</i> mutant (<i>ptsI316</i>) which has less than 1% residual PtsI activity is unable to ferment the PTS sugars glucose, fructose, mannose, mannitol, sorbitol, N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetyl mannosamine and the non-PTS sugars glycerol, melibiose, maltose and lactose [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/789368">Simoni76</a>].
<p>
Reviews: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9084757">Chauvin96a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11795882">Ginsburg02</a>].

<common-name datatype="string">DNA-binding transcriptional repressor MngR</common-name>

<comment datatype="string">According to microarray analysis, the "<b>m</b>a<b>n</b>nosyl-d-<b>g</b>lycerate <b>r</b>egulator," MngR, regulates only two genes, <i>mngA</i> and <i>mngB</i>, involved in 2-<i>O</i>-&alpha;-mannosyl-D-glycerate utilization [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14645248">Sampaio04</a>].  This regulator also autoregulates its own synthesis [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7805834">Quail94a</a>].
<p>
Previously, MngR, also called FarR, for <i>f</i>atty <i>a</i>cyl-<i>r</i>esponsive <i>r</i>egulator, had been proposed to regulate genes involved in the citric acid cycle in response to fatty acids, which release MngR from its DNA-binding site [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7805834">Quail94a</a>].  However, when it was found that this protein only regulates two genes, the suggestion was rejected and it was proposed that probably high concentrations of fatty acids could degrade the protein instead of it binding to the regulator [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14645248">Sampaio04</a>].  
<p>
MngR belongs to the GntR family of transcriptional regulators and has a helix-turn-helix motif in the N-terminal domain and a UbiC transcription regulator-associated domain that is predicted to be a sensor for small molecules.  This domain is found in proteins such as UbiC from <i>Escherichia coli</i>, TreR from <i>Bacillus subtilis</i>, and HutC from <i>Pseudomonas aeruginosa</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12757941">Aravind03</a>].
<p>
The <i>mntR</i> gene is transcribed divergently from the <i>mngAB</i> operon.  They share a regulatory region that contains two sites of 21 bp each, one with two direct repeat sequences of 10 bp that are bound by MngR [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7805834">Quail94a</a>].
<p>
<i>mngR</i> shows differential codon adaptation, resulting in differential translation efficiency signatures, in thermophilic microbes.  It was therefore predicted to play a role in the heat shock response.  An <i>mngR</i> deletion mutant was shown to be more sensitive than wild-type specifically to heat shock, but not other stresses [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24580753">Krisko14</a>].</comment>

<common-name datatype="string">DNA-binding transcriptional dual regulator FNR</common-name>

<comment datatype="string">FNR is the primary transcriptional regulator that mediates the transition from aerobic to anaerobic growth through the regulation of hundreds of genes. Generally, this protein activates genes involved in anaerobic metabolism and represses genes involved in aerobic metabolism [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12754220">Salmon03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15659690">Kang05a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32955440">Ireland20</a>]. FNR also regulates the transcription of many genes with other functions, such as acid resistance, chemotaxis, cell structure, and molecular biosynthesis, among others [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12754220">Salmon03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15659690">Kang05a</a>].
<p>
The cellular concentration of FNR is similar under both anaerobic and aerobic growth [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15547274">Sutton04</a>], but its activity is regulated directly by oxygen. A binding signature from FNR was observed only in low oxygen conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32955440">Ireland20</a>]. Under anaerobiosis, FNR acquires a [4Fe-4S] cluster that causes a conformational change and dimerization of the protein that causes it to become activated [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11581261">Moore01</a>]. Purification of [4Fe-4S]-FNR in an O<sub>2</sub>-free environment has been described [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19892202">Yan09a</a>]. The presence of O<sub>2</sub> results in inactivation of FNR via oxidation of this [4Fe-4S] cluster into a [2Fe-2S] cluster [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19261852">Jervis09</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15547274">Sutton04</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177174">Khoroshilova97</a>] and the disassembly of the dimer [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8576252">Lazazzera96</a>]. After prolonged O<sub>2</sub> exposure, the [2Fe-2S] cluster is destroyed, and apo-FNR, which lacks an Fe-S cluster, is the primary form of FNR under aerobiosis [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18055593">Reinhart08</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14730984">Sutton04a</a>]. Nitric oxide (NO) is also able to inactivate FNR through the nitrosylation of the [4Fe-4S] cluster, although NO is sensed by other transcription factors, and FNR appears only to function as a final safeguard against NO damage [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23471974">Crack13</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12093725">CruzRamos02</a>]. The phylogenetic relationship of the [4Fe-4S]-containing O<sub>2</sub> sensor was analyzed in bacteria [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30225854">Barth18</a>].
<p>
Based on mass spectrometry, intermediates between the O<sub>2</sub>-driven [4Fe-4S] to [2Fe-2S] conversion, such as [3Fe-3S] and [2Fe-2S](S)<sub>n</sub>, have been identified [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28373574">Crack17</a>]. Kinetic data showed that cluster sulfide oxidation occurred in parallel with cluster conversion [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28373574">Crack17</a>].
<p>
The accumulation of the protein FNR is slightly increased during iron-limiting conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31235512">Zupok19</a>].
<p>
Under ampicillin treatment, the activity of FNR appears to increase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33731833">Deter21</a>].
<p>
Under aerobiosis, the apo-FNR monomer is exposed and can be degraded by the ClpXP protease [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16243354">Mettert05</a>]. Two motifs of FNR appear to be necessary for this degradation, one located  in the N-terminal region and the other in the C-terminal region [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16243354">Mettert05</a>].
<p>
The activated FNR conformation is able to bind a specific palindromic sequence of DNA  with the consensus sequence TTGATNNNNATCAA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11771123">Gerasimova01</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2677602">Eiglmeier89</a>]. The G and the first T of each FNR half-site appears to interact with FNR residues Glu-209 and Ser-212 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2136332">Spiro90</a>]. FNR activates the transcription from class I and class II promoters, in which the FNR-binding sites are located  around -61, -71, -82, or -92 in class I and around -41.5 in class II [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7592457">Wing95</a>].  In class I promoters the second N and in class II promoters the third N of the consensus FNR site tend to be an A-T [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12706827">Scott03a</a>].
<p>
During activation, three activating regions (AR) are surface exposed for contact with the polymerase and promote transcription. The AR1 region contacts with the &alpha; subunit [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10972822">Lee00h</a>], the AR2 region makes contact with the &sigma;<sup>70</sup> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12374818">Blake02</a>], and the AR3 contacts the &alpha; NTD of the RNA polymerase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11786011">Lamberg02</a>]. The group amino acids Thr-118 with Ser-187; Lys-49 with Lys50; and Asp86 and Ile81 with Gly-85 are important for AR1, AR2, and AR3, respectively, to make contact with the RNA polymerase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10972822">Lee00h</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12374818">Blake02</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11786011">Lamberg02</a>]. The monomer in the FNR dimer that makes contact with the RNA polymerase and the activating region in FNR that makes the contact depends on the class of promoter, class I or class II [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10972822">Lee00h</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12374818">Blake02</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11786011">Lamberg02</a>].
<p>
FNR belongs to the CRP/FNR superfamily of transcription factors whose members are widely distributed in bacteria [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14638413">Korner03</a>].  These proteins have an N-terminal sensory domain, a C-terminal helix-turn-helix DNA-binding domain, and a dimerization motif in between [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14638413">Korner03</a>]. The sensory domain of FNR contains five cysteine residues, four of which are essential for linking the [4Fe-4S] cluster [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8497198">Green93</a>]. 
<p>
The intrinsic curvature and flexibility of binding sites of FNR were investigated. FNR showed higher levels of intrinsic curvature than the NAPs, such as IHF, H-NS, Fis, and Dps, and this curvature of binding sites is independent of the sequence-level conservation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29625128">Liu18c</a>]. The binding sites for FNR have high intrinsic curvature compared with flanking regions, and these are characterized by high structural flexibility  [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29625128">Liu18c</a>].
<p>
Under anaerobic growth conditions, transcription of the <i>fnr</i> gene is negatively autoregulated [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17293415">Mettert07</a>]. The growth [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28573283">Kargeti17</a>] and the net final biomass produced in an <i>fnr</i> single deletion mutant strain growing under anaerobic fermentation conditions were affected relative to responses of the wild-type strain (<i>Escherichia coli</i> strain BW25113) grown in the same conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28573283">Kargeti17</a>].The <i>fnr </i> mutant also caused decreased nucleotide synthesis, decreased glucose and ammonia uptake rates, and enhanced nitrogen transport and accumulation of amino acids and their precursors, as well as derepression of aerobic TCA cycle and alternate carbon metabolic proteins [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>]. The activities of some transcription factors appear to be enhanced (ArgR, NtrC, NrdR) or diminished (PuuR) in the fnr mutant [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>]. [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29748694">Kargeti18</a>] et al. reported a relative increase in the glucose uptake rate above that required for the observed growth rate. In addition, higher ATP synthesis and redox balance rates were reported relative to the observed growth rate and biomass yield in the mutant [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29748694">Kargeti18</a>].
<p>
Various target genes of FNR were found downregulated after 10 min of exposure to 2.5 mM H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, while the <i>fnr</i> gene was slightly upregulated [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35453340">Roth22</a>].
<p>
FNR was named for the mutant defect in "<b>f</b>umarate and <b>n</b>itrate <b>r</b>eduction" [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/796407">Lambden76</a>].  <i>fnr</i> mutants, also known as type III mutants, had originally been given the locus name <i>frdB</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/773363">Bachmann76</a>].
<p>
A new variant of FNR, (FNRD154A)<sub>2</sub>, was used to identify FNR interactions on the <i>ydfZ</i> promoter region [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22326866">Shan12</a>].  (FNRD154A)<sub>2</sub> also recognizes an FNR-dependent promoter under aerobic conditions and maintains its promoter specificity and conformational stability.  This variant was designed with enhanced stability to O<sub>2</sub>.  It could have a major impact on <i>in vitro</i> verification of the vast numbers of previously unrecognized genes in the FNR regulon, especially in genomic studies [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22326866">Shan12</a>].
<p>
Using  information available in EcoCyc and RegulonDB, 393 CRP feed-forward loops (FFLs) were identified. Microarray analyses revealed dynamic gene expression of each target in response to a range of cAMP dosages; eight types of FFLs were identified, and they were divided into five functional groups [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30096859">Yang18d</a>].
<p>
A variation at the F186 residue of FNR (F1861) causes a reduction of intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) and enhanced resistance to ionizing radiation under chronic exposure conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30673695">Bruckbauer19</a>].
The transcription of FNR-activatable promoters is reduced with the FNR variant  (F1861) under reduced oxygen, and cellular growth is enhanced in rich medium in the presence of the variant F1861[<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30673695">Bruckbauer19</a>].
<p>
A review of the regulation of molybdenum cofactor (Moco) biosynthesis and molybdoenzyme gene expression via molybdenum and iron by FNR, NarXL/QP, Fur, and ArcA has been published [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31517366">Zupok19a</a>].
<p>
Reviews: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18433630">Crack08</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14638413">Korner03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9990723">Kiley98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11931557">Unden02</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19246238">Green09</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28573283">Kargeti17</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>]</comment>

<common-name datatype="string">Fur-Fe<SUP>2+</SUP> DNA-binding transcriptional dual regulator</common-name>

<comment datatype="string">The transcriptional activator FUR, for "<b>F</b>erric <b>U</b>ptake <b>R</b>egulation,"  is capable of controlling its own synthesis [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3079747">Coulton86</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17921503">Chen07a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10411720">Newman99</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2836193">De88b</a>] and controls the transcription of genes involved in iron homeostasis [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11282473">Hantke01a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11101675">Vassinova00</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12475930">DAutreaux02</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9575233">Angerer98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17921503">Chen07a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8407793">Kammler93</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10411720">Newman99</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2644221">Griggs89</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15101990">Outten04</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2162465">Sauer90</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3294800">deLorenzo87</a>] and a minor sigma factor that initiates transcription of ferric citrate transport genes in response to the presence of periplasmic iron(III) dicitrate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17921503">Chen07a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12860393">Arechaga03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9575233">Angerer98</a>]. This regulator also participates in the regulation of transcription of many other genes involved in different cellular functions, including the following: flagellum chemotaxis [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8107138">Stojiljkovic94</a>], methionine biosynthesis [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8107138">Stojiljkovic94</a>], acid and oxidative stresses [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8412671">Tardat93</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11101675">Vassinova00</a>], metal ion stress [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11466284">Patzer01</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17120142">Koch07</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12480884">Puskarova02</a>], resistance to cobalt and nickel [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17129142">Sumi06</a>], the tricarboxylic acid cycle [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9418241">Tseng97</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15659676">Zhang05e</a>], glycolysis and gluconeogenesis [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11101675">Vassinova00</a>], respiration [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8107138">Stojiljkovic94</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9418241">Tseng97</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15659676">Zhang05e</a>], porins [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15659676">Zhang05e</a>], purine metabolism [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8107138">Stojiljkovic94</a>], 2,3-dihydroxybenzoate biosynthesis [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2139473">Brickman90</a>], and phage DNA packaging [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11101675">Vassinova00</a>]. Based on transcriptome analysis, expression levels of a set of genes regulated by Fur change substantially in response to antibiotic treatment  [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25063442">Mehi14</a>]. Iron homeostasis influences the evolution of ciprofloxacin resistance [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25063442">Mehi14</a>].
<p>
FUR is a transcriptional repressor but also can be an activator; the positive regulation of this regulator  is mediated by the indirect effect of RhyB, which is an antisense small RNA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17216355">Lee07z</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12975324">Masse03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16982641">Semsey06a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16199566">Masse05</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11917098">Masse02</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14617150">Vecerek03</a>].
<p>
FUR is a sensor  of  the concentration of intracellular iron, and the genetic repression occurs when the physiological inducer, iron (Fe<sup>2+</sup>), binds to FUR. This cofactor is required for DNA binding [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16216078">Mills05b</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17216355">Lee07z</a>]. FUR also is considered a  metalloregulatory protein and can sense different  divalent metal ions, such as Zn(II), Cu(II), Cd(II), Co(II), and Mn(II) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3294800">deLorenzo87</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10350474">Althaus99</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17216355">Lee07z</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11895294">Clarke01a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16216078">Mills05b</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16690618">Pecqueur06</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19023664">Jabour09</a>]. Transcriptomic and statistical modeling analyses with Zn concentration shifts showed a transient change in the activity of the iron regulator Fur and of the oxidative stress regulator SoxS; these findings suggest a competitive binding mechanism for the physiology of Zn and Fe uptake [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22016571">Graham12</a>]. On the other hand, D'Autreaux et al. showed that nitric oxide, a radical that is potentially toxic, inhibits  the DNA binding of this repressor [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16417522">Spiro06</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12475930">DAutreaux02</a>].
<p>
During iron starvation,  Fur is inactivated by the proteins YdiV and SlyD in a cooperative manner. They cause a conformational change in Fur that prevents its binding to DNA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32813023">Zhang20c</a>].
<p>
In the presence of iron, FUR binds in tandem to possible inverted repeat sequences in the  intergenic region to repress transcription by overlapping the -35 box of the regulated promoter. The FUR-binding sites were previously represented as regions of 19 bp, which were determined by footprinting of several promoter sequences [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3294800">deLorenzo87</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2644221">Griggs89</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8107138">Stojiljkovic94</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2015825">Saito91</a>]. Different aligments and computational analysis of these sequences showed different overlapping 15-bp sequences: TGATAATnATTATCA, consisting of two inverted repeats of 7 bp separated by 1 bp [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12374814">Baichoo02</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17921503">Chen07a</a>]. Experimental support for this consensus sequence was obtained from footprinting, site-directed mutagenesis experiments, analysis of the affinity and stoichiometry of DNA binding, gel retardation assays, etc. [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12374814">Baichoo02</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12644489">Lavrrar03</a>]. Currently there are different interpretations and models to explain how FUR could overlap inverted repeats in tandem [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12374814">Baichoo02</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17921503">Chen07a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12644489">Lavrrar03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16443380">Hamed06</a>].
<p>
Under anaerobic and iron-dependent growth conditions, Fur binds to more sites across the genome, increasing the number of target genes and its repressor effect. Four operons are regulated by Fur exclusively under these conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26670385">Beauchene15</a>]. Strains lacking Fur grow slower under aerobic conditions than under anaerobic conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26670385">Beauchene15</a>] , which suggests that Fur is controlled by O<sub>2</sub>. O<sub>2</sub> has a direct effect on levels of active Fur <i>in vivo</i>, and several factors contribute to the expression profile of the Fur regulon in response to O<sub>2</sub>, such as upregulation of FeoABC Fe<sup>2+</sup> uptake under anaerobic conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29087312">Beauchene17</a>]. Based on work with mutants and a predicted model, it was determined that when the intracellular free iron content is elevated, Fur protein reversibly binds a [2Fe-2S] cluster  to sense intracellular iron homeostasis via conserved cysteine residues  (Cys-93, Cys-96, Cys-113) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32928958">Fontenot20</a>].This fact raises the possibility that Fur can sense iron via [2Fe-2S] instead of via Fe<sup>2+</sup> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33188081">Lill20</a>].
<p>
Under ampicillin treatment, the activity of Fur appears to increase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33731833">Deter21</a>].
<p>
A role of Fur in the H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> response was suggested based on RNA-seq analysis [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35453340">Roth22</a>], as various genes repressed by Fur were found upregulated after 10 min of exposure to 2.5 mM H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> in comparison with controls, while after 60 min of exposure their transcription levels returned to baseline [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35453340">Roth22</a>]. However, transcription of the <i>fur</i> gene was found to be slightly upregulated, suggesting that Fur activity itself is repressed in the presence of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35453340">Roth22</a>].  
<p>
Review, with focus on the crystal structure of the Fur family of metalloregulators and its new structures bound to DNA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30014354">Sarvan18</a>]. A review of the regulation of molybdenum cofactor (Moco) biosynthesis and molybdoenzyme gene expression via molybdenum and iron by FNR, NarXL/QP, Fur, and ArcA has been published [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31517366">Zupok19a</a>].
<p>
A positive correlation between cellular growth and the copy number of the protein Fur has been reported [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35694815">Parisutham22</a>]. 
<p>
The expression of <i>fur</i> is reduced under iron limitation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31634530">Zhang19g</a>].</comment>

<common-name datatype="string">phosphocarrier protein HPr</common-name>

<comment datatype="string">HPr (histidine containing protein [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5545082">Kundig71a</a>]) is one of two sugar-non-specific protein constituents of the phosphoenolpyruvate:sugar phosphotransferase system (PTS<sup>sugar</sup>).  It accepts a phosphoryl group from phosphorylated Enzyme I (PtsI-P) and then transfers it to the EIIA domain of any one of the many sugar-specific enzymes (collectively known as Enzymes II) of the PTS<sup>sugar</sup> (reviewed in [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8246840">Postma93</a>]).
<p>
HPr is a small monomeric, single domain, protein that is relatively heat stable [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4942330">Anderson71a</a>]. HPr is phosphorylated at the N-1 position of histidine residue 15 (His-15) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4942330">Anderson71a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7803390">Rajagopal94</a>]. Phosphorylated HPr transfers its phosphate to the active histidine of the sugar transporters of the PTS<sup>sugar</sup>. Solution structures of the complex between HPr and the N-terminal domain of Enzyme I [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10048929">Garrett99</a>], and between HPr and the EIIA domain/protein of the glucose-specific PTS [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11060015">Wang00f</a>], the mannitol PTS [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12202490">Cornilescu02</a>] and the mannose PTS [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15788390">Williams05a</a>] have been obtained. HPr uses a consensus surface to interact with the varying proteins of the PTS<sup>sugar</sup> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10764730">Wang00j</a>]. 
<p>
Preferential utilization of glucose over mannitol is dependent upon HPr; dephosphorylated HPr, which accumulates during glucose transport, interacts specifically with <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=PD00369">MtlR</a> and enhances its repressor activity resulting in the inhibition of mannitol utilization [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28225088">Choe17</a>] (further [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31558743">Choe19</a>]).    
<p>
Purified HPr binds to, and enhances the oligomeric associations of <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=GLYCOPHOSPHORYL-MONOMER">glycogen phosphorylase (GlgP)</a>; HPr stimulates GlgP activity <i>in vitro</i> (decreased <i>K</i><sub>m</sub> for glycogen; increased <i>V</i><sub>max</sub> for phosphate); phosphorylated HPr has 4-fold higher affinity for GlgP than the unphosphorylated form, but does not appear to stimulate GlgP activity [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9334229">Seok97</a>] (see also [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11361069">Seok01</a>]). The unphosphorylated form of HPr binds to the anti-sigma factor, <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=EG11738-MONOMER">Rsd</a> with high affinity; dephosphorylated HPr interacts with and sequesters Rsd from &sigma;<sup>70</sup> <i>in vitro</i>; dephosphorylated HPr antagonizes Rsd activity resulting in increased &sigma;<sup>70</sup> dependent transcription and decreased &sigma;<sup>S</sup>-dependent transcription <i>in vivo</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24324139">Park13a</a>] (see also [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26457424">Park15c</a>]). HPr copurifies with the AI-2 kinase <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=G6798-MONOMER">LsrK</a>; HPr inhibits LsrK activity <i>in vitro</i>; phosphorylated HPr has a reduced ability to inhibit LsrK activity; HPr mediated regulation of LsrK may link sugar metabolism to quorum sensing activity [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29868643">Ha18</a>]. HPr is an allosteric activator of <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=PKI-MONOMER">pyruvate kinase 1</a>, <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=6PFK-2-MONOMER">6-phosphofructokinase 2</a> and <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=GLUCOSAMINE-6-P-DEAMIN-MONOMER">glucosamine-6-phosphate deaminase</a>; phosphorylated HPr is an allosteric inhibitor of <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=ADENYL-KIN-MONOMER">adenylate kinase</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28634232">Rodionova17</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29229699">Rodionova18</a>]. 
<p>
Both of the general PTS proteins - PtsI and PtsH - localize mainly near the cell poles [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20924357">Lopian10</a>].   
<p>
Phosphoryl flux through PTS systems (via Enzyme I and HPr) plays a regulatory role in coordinating carbon utilization strategy and more specifically in switching between the two alternative metabolic strategies of hierarchical sugar utilization versus co-utilization [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26784570">Westermayer16</a>].
<p>
Reviews: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9923705">Waygood98</a>]
<BR>Related reviews: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11361064">Peterkofsky01</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21621292">Gabor11</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22573269">Escalante12</a>]
<p>
</comment>

<common-name datatype="string">&alpha;-mannosidase</common-name>

<comment datatype="string">MngB is an &alpha;-mannosidase that appears to be responsible for the conversion of 2-<i>O</i>-(6-phospho-&alpha;-mannosyl)-D-glycerate (MG-P) to mannose-6-phosphate and glycerate in the <a href="/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY0-1300">2-<I>O</I>-&alpha;-mannosyl-D-glycerate degradation</a> pathway [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14645248">Sampaio04</a>].  The enzyme has not yet been purified and assayed <i>in vitro</i>. 
<p>
Expression of <i>mngAB</i> is repressed by MngR and induced when cells are grown in 2-<i>O</i>-&alpha;-mannosyl-D-glycerate (MG).  <i>mngB</i> mutants are unable to grow in medium containing high levels of MG (without secondary mutations in <i>mngA</i>), likely due to the toxicity of accumulating MG-P within the cells [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14645248">Sampaio04</a>].
<p>
MngB: "<b>m</b>a<b>n</b>nosyl<b>g</b>lycerate catabolism <b>B</b>" [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14645248">Sampaio04</a>]</comment>

<common-name datatype="string">Inferred from genetic interaction</common-name>
<comment datatype="string">IGI inferred from genetic interaction.

<br>
The assertion was inferred from a genetic interaction such as
<ul>
    <li> "Traditional" genetic interactions such as suppressors, synthetic lethals, etc.
    <li> Functional complementation
    <li> Inference about one gene drawn from the phenotype of a mutation in a different gene
</ul><p class=ecocomment>
This category includes any combination of alterations in the sequence
(mutation) or expression of more than one gene/gene product. This
category can therefore cover any of the IMP experiments that are done
in a non-wild-type background, although we prefer to use it only when
all mutations are documented. When redundant copies of a gene must all
be mutated to see an informative phenotype, use the IGI code. (Yes, 
this implies some organisms, such as mouse, will have far, far more IGI
than IMP annotations.)<p class=ecocomment>
<p>
IMP also covers phenotypic similarity: a phenotype that is informative
because it is similar to that of another independent phenotype (which
may have been described earlier or documented more fully) is IMP (not IGI).<p class=ecocomment>
<p>
We have also decided to use this category for situations where a
mutation in one gene (gene A) provides information about the function,
process, or component of another gene (gene B; i.e. annotate gene B
using IGI).
</comment>
</Evidence-Code>
